newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela ends Venalum dispute with Japanese.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela ends Venalum dispute with Japanese.

text.p: Venezuela has reached an agreement and ended a dispute with a Japanese consortium that owns 20 percent of aluminium smelter Venalum, Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said on Thursday.
"An agreement was reached with the Japanese in the Venalum case, which is great news," Petkoff told reporters after a seminar at the Caracas Stock Exchange.
Petkoff said he received the news in a telephone call from New York by Elas Ynaty, president of state-run Corporacin Venezolana de Guayana (CVG), which owns 80 percent of Venalum.

Venezuelan officials started three days of talks Tuesday in New York with representatives of the Japanese consortium led by Showa Denko KK. At stake was the Japanese consortium's power of veto over the 430,000 tonnes per year capacity smelter.
Petkoff added that the agreement will allow "the full success of the privatization of aluminium firms at the end of the year."
Petkoff gave no details of what the accord entailed.
The New York talks followed negotiations in Tokyo last month that broke down without an agreement.
The dispute started at the beginning of the year over a provision that gave the Japanese side veto power over major Venalum decisions.
In exchange for the removal of this veto power, the Japanese wanted compensation and asked Venezuela to re-start shipments of a 90,000 tonnes per year contract, which was suspended in February.

The Venezuelan government was eager to find a solution because the dispute was delaying its plan to sell in December a controlling stake in Venalum, along with smelter Alcasa, carbon anode producer Carbonorca and bauxite and alumina firm Bauxilum.
Analysts have valued the four companies at about $2 billion.
Apart from Showa Denko KK, the Japanese consortium includes Kobe Steel Ltd, Sumimoto Chemical Co Ltd, Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Mitsubishi Aluminium Co Ltd and Marubeni Corp.
